query: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr exhibits 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility in the cast state and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C at strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1, but inadequate oxygen resistance prevents most practical high-temperature applications. Earlier oxidation-protection research prevented pesting in a related, non-equiatomic Hf–Nb–Ta–Ti–Zr alloy during a 5 h exposure to air at 800 °C, but that result does not establish protection for equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr; related studies on other refractory alloys likewise did not evaluate this composition. With preservation of useful room- and high-temperature mechanical performance as a design constraint, what single intervention could improve the oxygen resistance of equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr? Formulate one hypothesis identifying the intervention and mechanism, predicting the outcome relative to untreated material, defining the applicable temperature, atmosphere, exposure-time, and loading boundaries, citing supporting evidence from the prior studies, and specifying a controlled experiment and result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A post‐cast, low‐energy Cr ion implantation treatment that creates a thin Cr‐rich surface layer on equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr will promote the in situ formation of a continuous, adherent CrTaO4‐based oxide during high‐temperature exposure, thereby significantly enhancing its oxidation resistance without altering its intrinsic room‐ and high‐temperature mechanical performance.
generation.material_initial_state: As‐cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr with known ductility (8–16% tensile ductility at room temperature) and yield strength (163–530 MPa at 1000 °C) but with inadequate oxygen resistance.
generation.intervention: Apply a low‐energy Cr ion implantation (or equivalently a controlled, thin Cr surface deposition) to create a Cr-enriched surface layer prior to high-temperature service.
generation.conditions: Exposure in air at 800–1000 °C for durations up to 100 hours; mechanical performance evaluated at room temperature and under high-temperature conditions at strain rates of 10^−4–10^−2 s^−1.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a stable, dense, and adherent CrTaO4 (or related Cr-containing mixed oxide) scale along the treated surface that acts as a barrier to oxygen ingress.
generation.mechanism: The Cr-rich surface will preferentially oxidize to form a protective oxide that slows further oxygen diffusion into the bulk. This surface reaction is expected to occur without substantial solute redistribution in the interior, hence preserving the inherent ductility and yield strength of the alloy.
generation.predicted_outcome: Samples receiving the Cr ion implantation will show substantially reduced oxidation weight gain and improved oxide scale adhesion during extended isothermal oxidation at 800–1000 °C compared to untreated specimens, while retaining similar room‐ and high‐temperature mechanical properties.
generation.baseline: Untreated equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr, which exhibits rapid disintegration (pesting) due to uncontrolled oxidation under high‐temperature air exposure, compromising its practical high-temperature applications.
generation.boundary: The intervention is applicable under high-temperature air exposure (800–1000 °C for up to 100 h) and is intended for cast specimens where mechanical performance (ductility and yield strength) must not be degraded by any compositional modification. The protective effect is evaluated in the as-cast bulk, not by later bulk alloying.
generation.uncertainty: This hypothesis extends the evidence from studies showing that (i) the addition of Cr in RHEA coatings (PMC10142552) leads to improved formation of protective oxides and (ii) surface treatments such as electrospark deposition have been effective in related HfNbTaTiZr systems (PMC8348113). What is new is using a controlled Cr ion implantation to create a sub-micrometer surface enriched layer that triggers the formation of a protective CrTaO4-type oxide without altering the intrinsic bulk composition—a strategy not yet explored for equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr. Uncertainties remain regarding the long-term stability and adhesion of the implanted layer under cyclic thermal stress.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of as-cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr samples; one set receives low-energy Cr ion implantation to form a thin (sub-micron) Cr-enriched surface layer, while the other set remains untreated. Subject both groups to isothermal oxidation tests in air at 800 °C for 100 hours. Following oxidation, conduct microstructural (SEM/TEM) and compositional analyses of the oxide scales, and perform tensile tests at room temperature and high temperature (near 1000 °C) to evaluate any changes in ductility and yield strength.
measurements: Oxidation weight gain as a function of time
Morphology and composition of the oxide scale (via SEM, TEM, EDS, XRD)
Tensile ductility and yield strength before and after oxidation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis will be falsified if (a) the Cr-treated specimens do not exhibit at least a 30% reduction in oxidation weight gain relative to controls, (b) the protective oxide scale is found to be non-uniform, discontinuous, or spalls readily, or (c) the treated samples show a statistically significant (>10%) degradation in tensile ductility or yield strength compared to untreated specimens.

cited_evidence.text: Weight gain (mg/cm2) and weight-gain rate (mg/(cm2·h)) of WVTaTiCrx RHEA coating after oxidation at 800 °C for 50 h are shown in Table 3. When Cr is not added, the weight gain and oxidation rate of the WVTaTi high-entropy alloy coating oxide are 10.41 mg/cm2 and 0.21 mg/(cm2·h), respectively. With the increase in Cr content, the weight increases of oxide on the coating surface decreases. The addition of Cr resulted in the smallest increase in oxidation weight of the Cr1 RHEA coating, with a mass increase of 5.12 mg/cm2 and an oxidation rate of 0.10 mg/(cm2·h). According to the oxidation-resistance rating standard of steel, superalloy, and high-temperature protective coatings (HB5258-2000) [], it can be seen that Cr1 RHEA coating belongs to the antioxidant alloys, and Cr0.25, Cr0.5, and Cr0.75 belong to the sub-antioxidant alloys. In general, the proper addition of the Cr element can effectively improve the oxidation resistance of the coating.

Among these alloys, HfMoNbTaTi has the best mechanical performance, that is, 27% compressive strain at room temperature and yield strength 367 MPa at 1400 °C. HfMoNbTaTi has great potential for elevated-temperature applications. As the alloy system does not contain very expensive elements such as Re and Ru, it is cost competitive for high-temperature applications like Nb-Hf-Ti alloys in space vehicles. Further modification of composition and/or anti-oxidation coatings are still required for high-temperature applications in the air.
